newsitem.title: CANADA: Bell Canada head wants more deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Bell Canada head wants more deregulation.

text.p: John McLennan, chief executive of BCE Inc unit Bell Canada, said on Tuesday that he wanted more and faster deregulation of the Canadian telecommunications industry.

Speaking to reporters after a speech, McLennan welcomed the announcement by the Canadian government that it offered in WTO negotiations to end the Teleglobe Inc monopoly on overseas telephone traffic from Canada by October 1, 1998.
"I think the lifting of the monopoly is absolutely the right thing. We would have liked to have seen it happen a lot sooner," McLennan said.

Teleglobe said it also welcomed the Canadian government's initiative because it favored a WTO agreement in Geneva, where talks were being held, that would set multilateral ground rules for basic telecommunications services.

"We see it as a significant improvement for the WTO negotiations and think it is an important move from the government's part in trying to secure an agreement in Geneva," Teleglobe spokesman Mark Boutet told Reuters.
Teleglobe asked in late 1995 that its Canadian monopoly on overseas traffic not be renewed.

Teleglobe benefits from the reciprocal deregulation of long-distance services in other markets such as the United States where last year it was awarded a telecommunications reseller's license and facilities-based provider's license.

McLennan said net disbursements to Teleglobe from the Stentor group of Canadian telephone companies, which includes Bell Canada, the country's largest, totaled more than C$500 million a year. Stentor has a 10-year contract with Teleglobe ending in 2003, in which Teleglobe agreed to charge prices matching U.S. benchmark prices.
Under the contract, the Stentor companies agreed to remain with Teleglobe for at least one year after the end of Teleglobe's monopoly.
McLennan said he wanted faster deregulation of the Canadian telecommunications market to let Bell Canada offer packages of domestic and long-distance services.

"What I would like to be able to do right away is package long distance, wireless services with Bell Mobility, Internet access and some other special features...and give it a flat rate price," McLennan said.
McLennan said it might take Canadian regulators 18 more months to allow the Stentor companies to custom package such services for their customers.
